cor-extend-orthonormal-basis.title: Extending an Orthonormal List
cor-extend-orthonormal-basis.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let (e1,…,er) be an orthonormal list in V. Then there are vectors er+1,…,en∈V such that (e1,…,en) is an orthonormal basis of V.

cor-inner-product-spaces-isomorphic.title: Classification of Finite-Dimensional Inner Product Spaces
cor-inner-product-spaces-isomorphic.title_html: Classification of Finite-Dimensional Inner Product Spaces
cor-inner-product-spaces-isomorphic.html: Let V be an inner product space over F with dim⁡V=n. Then there is an isomorphism T:V→Fn with ⟨Tu,Tv⟩=⟨u,v⟩for all u,v∈V, where the right-hand inner product is that of V and the left-hand one is the standard inner product of Fn. An isomorphism with this property is an isometric isomorphism, so every n-dimensional inner product space over F is isometrically isomorphic to Fn.

cor-least-squares-unique.title: Uniqueness of the least-squares solution
cor-least-squares-unique.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and b∈Fm. The following are equivalent:

  1. Ax=b has exactly one least-squares solution (for one, equivalently for every, b);
  2. the columns of A are linearly independent, that is rankA=n;
  3. A∗A is invertible.

In that case the least-squares solution is x=(A∗A)−1A∗b.

cor-projection-orthogonal-basis.title: Projecting with an orthogonal basis
cor-projection-orthogonal-basis.html: Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V, and let (u1,…,uk) be an orthogonal basis of U, so that ⟨ui,uj⟩=0 for i≠j and every ui≠0. Then PUv=∑i=1k⟨v,ui⟩⟨ui,ui⟩uifor every v∈V.

cor-rank-adjoint.title: Rank of the Adjoint
cor-rank-adjoint.html:
Let V,W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F and T∈L(V,W). Then

  1. rankT∗=rankT;
  2. ker(T∗T)=kerT, and consequently rank(T∗T)=rankT.

cor-riesz-isomorphism.title: The Riesz map
cor-riesz-isomorphism.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F. Define Φ:V→V∗,Φ(w)=⟨⋅,w⟩. Then Φ is a bijection, and for all w,w′∈V and c∈F, Φ(w+w′)=Φ(w)+Φ(w′),Φ(cw)=c―Φ(w). In particular Φ is an isomorphism of vector spaces when F=R, and is conjugate-linear when F=C.

cor-triangle-inequality.title: Triangle Inequality
cor-triangle-inequality.html: Let V be an inner product space and u,v∈V. Then ‖u+v‖≤‖u‖+‖v‖.

def-adjoint.title: Adjoint
def-adjoint.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F and let T∈L(V,W). The adjoint of T is the unique linear map T∗∈L(W,V) satisfying ⟨Tv,w⟩=⟨v,T∗w⟩for all v∈V and all w∈W.

def-angle.title: Angle Between Vectors
def-angle.html: Let V be a real inner product space and let u,v∈V be non-zero. The angle between u and v is the unique θ∈[0,π] with cos⁡θ=⟨u,v⟩‖u‖‖v‖.

def-conjugate-transpose.title: Conjugate Transpose
def-conjugate-transpose.html: For A∈Mm×n(F), the conjugate transpose A∗∈Mn×m(F) is the matrix with entries (A∗)ij=aji―. A square matrix with A∗=A is Hermitian.

def-distance-to-subspace.title: Distance to a subspace
def-distance-to-subspace.html: Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V and let v∈V. The distance from v to U is d(v,U)=minu∈U‖v−u‖=‖v−PUv‖.

def-fourier-coefficients.title: Fourier Coefficients With Respect to an Orthonormal List
def-fourier-coefficients.title_html: Fourier Coefficients With Respect to an Orthonormal List
def-fourier-coefficients.html: Let (e1,…,ek) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space V and let v∈V. The scalars ⟨v,e1⟩, …, ⟨v,ek⟩∈F are the Fourier coefficients of v with respect to the list.

def-givens-rotation.title: Givens Rotation
def-givens-rotation.html: Let 1≤i<j≤m and let c,s∈R with c2+s2=1. The Givens rotation G(i,j;c,s)∈Mm(R) is the identity matrix with the four entries in rows and columns i,j replaced by (giigijgjigjj)=(cs−sc).

def-gram-matrix.title: Gram Matrix
def-gram-matrix.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space V over F. Its Gram matrix is G∈Mk(F) with entries (G)ij=⟨vj,vi⟩(1≤i,j≤k).

def-householder-reflection.title: Householder Reflection
def-householder-reflection.html: Let w∈Fm be non-zero. The Householder reflection determined by w is Hw=Im−2ww∗‖w‖2∈Mm(F).

def-induced-norm.title: Induced Norm
def-induced-norm.html: Let V be an inner product space. The norm of v∈V is ‖v‖:=⟨v,v⟩, the non-negative real square root. A vector with ‖v‖=1 is a unit vector, and replacing a non-zero v by v/‖v‖ is called normalizing it.

def-inner-product.title: Inner Product
def-inner-product.html:
Let F be R or C, and let V be a vector space over F. An inner product on V is a map ⟨⋅,⋅⟩:V×V→F such that for all u,v,w∈V and all a,b∈F:

  1. ⟨au+bv,w⟩=a⟨u,w⟩+b⟨v,w⟩ (linear in the first slot);
  2. ⟨v,u⟩=⟨u,v⟩― (conjugate symmetry);
  3. ⟨v,v⟩>0 for every non-zero v∈V (positive definiteness).

A vector space equipped with an inner product is an inner product space. When F=R it is a real inner product space, when F=C a complex one.

def-isometry.title: Isometry
def-isometry.html: Let V and W be inner product spaces over F. A linear map T∈L(V,W) is an isometry if ‖Tv‖=‖v‖for every v∈V.

def-normal-operator.title: Normal Operator
def-normal-operator.html: An operator T∈L(V) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is normal if it commutes with its adjoint: T∗T=TT∗.

def-orthogonal.title: Orthogonal Vectors
def-orthogonal.html: Let V be an inner product space. Vectors u,v∈V are orthogonal, written u⊥v, if ⟨u,v⟩=0. A list (v1,…,vk) is orthogonal if vi⊥vj whenever i≠j.

def-orthogonal-complement.title: Orthogonal complement
def-orthogonal-complement.html: Let V be an inner product space over F and let S⊆V be any subset. The orthogonal complement of S is S⊥={v∈V:⟨v,s⟩=0 for every s∈S}, read “S perp”.

def-orthogonal-polynomial-sequence.title: Orthogonal Polynomial Sequence
def-orthogonal-polynomial-sequence.html:
Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ be an inner product on R[x], or on R[x]≤n. An orthogonal polynomial sequence for it is a sequence p0,p1,p2,… of polynomials (a finite list p0,…,pn in the second case) such that

  1. deg⁡pk=k for every index k;
  2. ⟨pj,pk⟩=0 whenever j≠k.

The sequence is monic if every pk has leading coefficient 1.

def-orthogonal-projection.title: Orthogonal projection
def-orthogonal-projection.html: Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V. By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), every v∈V has a unique splitting v=u+w with u∈U and w∈U⊥. The orthogonal projection onto U is the operator PU∈L(V) defined by PUv=u.

def-orthonormal-basis.title: Orthonormal Basis
def-orthonormal-basis.html: An orthonormal basis of an inner product space V is an orthonormal list that is a basis of V.

def-orthonormal-list.title: Orthonormal List
def-orthonormal-list.html: Let V be an inner product space. A list (e1,…,ek) of vectors of V is orthonormal if ⟨ei,ej⟩=δijfor all i,j∈{1,…,k}, that is, if ⟨ei,ej⟩=0 whenever i≠j (orthogonal) and ‖ei‖=1 for every i (normalized).

def-self-adjoint.title: Self-adjoint Operator
def-self-adjoint.html: An operator T∈L(V) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is self-adjoint if T∗=T, that is, if ⟨Tu,v⟩=⟨u,Tv⟩for all u,v∈V. The matrix counterpart is the Hermitian matrix of @def-conjugate-transpose, A∗=A; over R this says A⊤=A, and the matrix is symmetric.

def-unitary-orthogonal.title: Unitary and Orthogonal
def-unitary-orthogonal.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F. An operator T∈L(V) is unitary if T∗T=TT∗=idV, equivalently if T is an invertible isometry. When F=R, such a T is also called orthogonal.

A matrix A∈Mn(C) with A∗A=In is a unitary matrix; a matrix A∈Mn(R) with A⊤A=In is an orthogonal matrix.

def-unitary-orthogonal-groups.title: The Unitary and Orthogonal Groups
def-unitary-orthogonal-groups.html: For n≥1 set U(n):={A∈Mn(C):A∗A=In},O(n):={A∈Mn(R):A⊤A=In}, and SO(n):={A∈O(n):detA=1}, the special orthogonal group.

exm-adjoint-differentiation.title: Differentiation on a Polynomial Space
exm-adjoint-differentiation.html: On V=R[x]≤2 define ⟨p,q⟩:=a0b0+a1b1+a2b2 for p=a0+a1x+a2x2 and q=b0+b1x+b2x2. (This is the standard inner product of R3 transported by the coordinate map, so it is an inner product, and E=(1,x,x2) is an orthonormal basis.) Find the adjoint of D:V→V, D(p)=p′.

  2. For f(x)=|x| and n=1, write out both sides of @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) using @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b1 (a), and show that the resulting inequality is equivalent to 96≤π4.

exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b3.title: B3: The best approximation by \Span(1, \cos x)
exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b3.title_html: B3: The best approximation by span(1,cos⁡x)
exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b3.html: In C[−π,π] with ⟨f,g⟩=1π∫−ππfg, let U=span(1,cos⁡x) and f(x)=x2. Find PUf and d(f,U)2. Hint: the list (1,cos⁡x) is orthogonal but not orthonormal.

exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c1.title: C1: Parseval for the full trigonometric system
exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c1.title_html: C1: Parseval for the full trigonometric system
exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c1.html:
This exercise uses an input from analysis that this book does not prove: the trigonometric system is complete in C[−π,π], meaning that for every f∈C[−π,π], a022+∑k=1∞(ak2+bk2)=1π∫−ππf(t)2dt.

  1. Apply this to f(x)=x and deduce that ∑k=1∞1/k2=π2/6.
  2. Hence deduce that ∑k=1∞1/(2k−1)2=π2/8.
  3. Say precisely which step used the analysis input, and explain why no result of this section can supply it.

exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c2.title: C2: Chebyshev orthogonality by substitution
exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-c2.html:
Let ⟨p,q⟩w=∫−11p(t)q(t)(1−t2)−1/2dt on R[x], the Chebyshev inner product of the text.

  1. Prove that for every n≥0 there is a polynomial Tn of degree n with Tn(cos⁡θ)=cos⁡nθ for all θ, and find T0,T1,T2,T3.
  2. Prove that ⟨p,q⟩w=∫0πp(cos⁡θ)q(cos⁡θ)dθ for all polynomials p,q.
  3. Deduce that ⟨Tm,Tn⟩w=0 for m≠n, and compute ⟨Tn,Tn⟩w.

Hint for (a): the identity cos⁡((n+1)θ)+cos⁡((n−1)θ)=2cos⁡θcos⁡nθ.

exr-inner-products-a1.title: A1
exr-inner-products-a1.html:
1. State the three axioms of an inner product on a vector space over F=R or C, and say in which slot the map is linear.
  2. Why must the field be R or C? Name the two features used.
  3. Explain why ⟨v,v⟩ is always a real number.
  4. True or false: an inner product on a complex space is linear in the second slot. Justify your answer.
  5. State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, its equality case, and one place where the equality case is used.
  6. True or false: if ‖u+v‖2=‖u‖2+‖v‖2 in a complex inner product space, then u⊥v. Justify your answer.

exr-inner-products-b1.title: B1: Determine which are inner products
exr-inner-products-b1.title_html: B1: Determine which are inner products
exr-inner-products-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are inner products on the stated space. For those that are, verify the axioms; for those that are not, name the clause that fails and give an explicit witness.

  1. On R2: ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+3x2y2.
  2. On R2: ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1+x1y2+x2y1+2x2y2.
  3. On C2: ⟨x,y⟩=x1y1―+x2y2.
  4. On M2(R): ⟨A,B⟩=tr(AB).
  5. On R[x]≤2: ⟨p,q⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2).

exr-inner-products-b2.title: B2: Norms and angles
exr-inner-products-b2.html:
1. In R3 with the dot product, find ‖u‖, ‖v‖ and the cosine of the angle between u=(1,2,2) and v=(2,−1,2).
  2. In R[x]≤2 with ⟨p,q⟩=∫−11pq, compute ‖1‖, ‖x‖ and ⟨1,x⟩. What is the angle between 1 and x?
  3. In M2(C) with the Frobenius inner product, compute ‖A‖ for A=(1i01+i).

exr-inner-products-b3.title: B3: Cauchy–Schwarz, concretely
exr-inner-products-b3.html:
1. Verify @thm-cauchy-schwarz for a=(1,2,3) and b=(3,2,1) in R3 with the dot product, and say whether the inequality is strict.
  2. Deduce from @thm-cauchy-schwarz the classical inequality (∑i=1naibi)2≤(∑i=1nai2)(∑i=1nbi2) for all real ai,bi.
  3. Hence show that (a1+⋯+an)2≤n(a12+⋯+an2) for all real ai.

exr-inner-products-b4.title: B4: A lower bound for a difference of norms
exr-inner-products-b4.title_html: B4: A lower bound for a difference of norms
exr-inner-products-b4.html: Let V be an inner product space and u,v∈V. Prove that |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖.

exr-inner-products-c1.title: C1: The parallelogram law characterizes inner-product norms
exr-inner-products-c1.title_html: C1: The parallelogram law characterizes inner-product norms
exr-inner-products-c1.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on R2, that is, a function R2→R satisfying the three properties of @thm-norm-properties (a), (b) and @cor-triangle-inequality. Suppose it satisfies the parallelogram law ‖u+v‖2+‖u−v‖2=2‖u‖2+2‖v‖2 for all u,v, and define β(u,v)=14(‖u+v‖2−‖u−v‖2).

  1. Show that β(u,u)=‖u‖2, that β(u,v)=β(v,u), and that β(u,0)=0.
  2. Prove that β(u,v)+β(u,w)=2β(u,12(v+w)) for all u,v,w.
  3. Deduce that β(u,v)+β(u,w)=β(u,v+w).
  4. Granting that β(u,tv)=tβ(u,v) for all t∈R, conclude that β is an inner product on R2 whose induced norm is ‖⋅‖.

Hint: for (b), apply the parallelogram law to the pair u+12(v+w), 12(v−w), and then to the pair u−12(v+w), 12(w−v).

exr-inner-products-c2.title: C2: Recovering the inner product from the norm
exr-inner-products-c2.title_html: C2: Recovering the inner product from the norm
exr-inner-products-c2.html:
Let V be an inner product space over F.

  1. For F=R, prove the polarization identity ⟨u,v⟩=14(‖u+v‖2−‖u−v‖2).
  2. For F=C, prove that ⟨u,v⟩=14∑k=03ik‖u+ikv‖2.
  3. Deduce that two inner products on V with the same induced norm are equal.

exr-inner-products-c3.title: C3: The equality cases
exr-inner-products-c3.html:
Let V be an inner product space.

  1. Prove that ‖u+v‖=‖u‖+‖v‖ if and only if one of u,v is a non-negative real multiple of the other.
  2. Deduce the equality condition in the classical inequality of @exr-inner-products-b3 (b): for real ai,bi, equality holds if and only if one of the vectors (a1,…,an), (b1,…,bn) is a multiple of the other.
  3. Give real numbers ai,bi, not all zero, with ∑aibi<0 and equality in the classical inequality, and explain why this does not contradict (a).

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-a1.title: A1
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-a1.html:
1. Define an isometry T∈L(V,W), and state two conditions equivalent to it.
  2. What must be checked about a square matrix A to decide whether it is unitary? State the check in terms of its columns.
  3. True or false: every isometry is invertible. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if detA=1 for A∈O(n), then A fixes a non-zero vector. Justify your answer.
  5. Give the two families of matrices making up O(2), and say how the determinant distinguishes them.
  6. An operator T on a complex inner product space is unitary. Why must every eigenvalue of T lie on the unit circle?

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b1.title: B1: Determine which are unitary
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b1.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are orthogonal or unitary. Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the failing condition.

  1. 13(2−21122−2−12) over R.
  2. 12(1ii1) over C.
  3. (1101) over R.
  4. 15(3443) over R.

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b2.title: B2: Name the plane isometry
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b2.html:
Each of the following lies in O(2). Decide whether it is a rotation or a reflection, and give the angle of rotation or the mirror line.

  1. (0110).
  2. 12(11−11).
  3. 113(51212−5).

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b3.title: B3: Permutations are orthogonal
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-b3.html:
Let σ∈Sn and let Pσ∈Mn(R) be its permutation matrix (@def-permutation-matrix), whose j-th column is eσ(j).

  1. Prove that Pσ∈O(n).
  2. Deduce that detPσ=±1, and identify the sign.
  3. Show that Pσ−1=Pσ⊤=Pσ−1.

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c1.title: C1: Determinant as a homomorphism
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c1.html:
1. Prove that det:O(n)→{1,−1} is a surjective group homomorphism with kernel SO(n), and deduce that exactly half of O(n) has determinant −1, in the sense that O(n) is the disjoint union of SO(n) and one coset A0SO(n).
  2. Prove that det:U(n)→{z∈C:|z|=1} is a surjective group homomorphism.
  3. Describe O(1) and U(1) completely.

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c2.title: C2: Linearity is a hypothesis, not a consequence
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c2.title_html: C2: Linearity is a hypothesis, not a consequence
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c2.html:
1. Let c:C→C be c(z)=z―, where C carries ⟨z,w⟩=zw―. Show that ‖c(z)‖=‖z‖ for every z, that c is not linear over C, and that c does not preserve the inner product. Which step of @thm-isometry-characterizations fails?
  2. Let V be a complex inner product space and let T∈L(V) satisfy ⟨Tv,v⟩=0 for every v∈V. Prove that T=0.
  3. Show that (b) fails over R by exhibiting a non-zero T∈L(R2) with ⟨Tv,v⟩=0 for all v.

Hint for (b): apply the hypothesis to v=u+w and to v=u+iw.

exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c3.title: C3: Two reflections make a rotation
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c3.title_html: C3: Two reflections make a rotation
exr-isometries-and-unitary-maps-c3.html:
Let α,β∈R and let Mα,Mβ∈O(2) be the reflections of @thm-orthogonal-2x2, in the lines Lα and Lβ at angles α/2 and β/2.

  1. Prove that MαMβ=Rα−β.
  2. Deduce that the composite of the reflections in two lines through the origin is the rotation by twice the angle from the second line to the first, and that every rotation of the plane is a product of two reflections.
  3. Deduce that O(2) is not abelian, by computing MβMα.

exr-least-squares-a1.title: A1
exr-least-squares-a1.html:
1. Define a least-squares solution of Ax=b, and write down the normal equations.
  2. True or false: if Ax=b is consistent, then its solutions are exactly its least-squares solutions. Justify your answer.
  3. Explain in one sentence why the normal equations are always consistent.
  4. Give a condition on the columns of A equivalent to uniqueness of the least-squares solution.
  5. Where does the minimum-norm solution of a consistent system live, and why is it unique there?
  6. True or false: (A∗A)−1=A−1(A∗)−1. Justify your answer.

exr-least-squares-b1.title: B1: A least-squares line
exr-least-squares-b1.html: Find the least-squares line y=c+dt for the data (0,3),(1,2),(2,3),(3,6). Compute the residual, verify that it is orthogonal to both columns of A, and give the minimum sum of squares.

exr-least-squares-b2.title: B2: A least-squares parabola
exr-least-squares-b2.html: Find the least-squares quadratic y=a+bt+ct2 for the data (−1,2),(0,8),(1,6),(2,16), and the minimum sum of squares. Hint: write down A⊤A from the power sums ∑tik, k=0,…,4.

exr-least-squares-b3.title: B3: A minimum-norm solution
exr-least-squares-b3.html: Find the minimum-norm solution of {x1+x3=2,x2+x3=3, and verify that it is orthogonal to nul(A).

exr-least-squares-c1.title: C1: Weighted least squares
exr-least-squares-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R), b∈Rm, and let w1,…,wm>0 be weights, with W=diag(w1,…,wm).

  1. Show that ⟨x,y⟩W=y⊤Wx is an inner product on Rm.
  2. Prove that the minimizers of ∑i=1mwi((Ax)i−bi)2 are exactly the solutions of A⊤WAx=A⊤Wb.
  3. For the data (0,2),(1,1),(2,8) with weights (1,2,1), find the weighted least-squares line, and compare it with the unweighted one.

exr-least-squares-c2.title: C2: The residual, two ways
exr-least-squares-c2.html:
Let x be a least-squares solution of Ax=b and let r=b−Ax.

  1. Prove that ‖r‖2=‖b‖2−‖Ax‖2, and also that ‖r‖2=⟨b,r⟩=‖b‖2−⟨A∗b,x⟩.
  2. Use the second formula to recompute the minimum sum of squares in @exm-least-squares-line without finding the residual vector.

exr-least-squares-c3.title: C3: A rank-deficient least-squares problem
exr-least-squares-c3.html:
Let A=(101011112),b=(120).

  1. Show that Ax=b is inconsistent and that rankA=2.
  2. Describe all least-squares solutions.
  3. Find the one of smallest norm, and the minimum sum of squares.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: A1
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html:
1. Define the orthogonal complement S⊥ of a subset S of an inner product space.
  2. True or false: S⊥ is a subspace only when S is a subspace. Justify your answer.
  3. State the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, including every hypothesis.
  4. Let U be a 3-dimensional subspace of R7. What is dim⁡U⊥, and what is dim⁡(U⊥)⊥?
  5. What quantity does PUv minimize, and over what set?
  6. Name two differences between U⊥ and the annihilator U0.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: B1: A complement and a projection in \nR^4
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title_html: B1: A complement and a projection in R4
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html:
In R4 with the dot product, let U=span((1,1,0,0), (0,0,1,1)).

  1. Find a basis of U⊥ and verify the dimension count.
  2. Compute PUv and d(v,U) for v=(1,2,3,4).
  3. Verify directly that v−PUv∈U⊥.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: B2: Distance from a point to a plane
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title_html: B2: Distance from a point to a plane
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html: In R3 with the dot product, let U={(x,y,z):2x−y+2z=0} and v=(1,2,3). Compute d(v,U) and PUv, and check that PUv lies in U. Hence write down the general formula for the distance from v to the plane {x:⟨x,n⟩=0}, n≠0.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: B3: The best quadratic approximation to a quartic
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title_html: B3: The best quadratic approximation to a quartic
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html: On R[x]≤4 with ⟨p,q⟩=∫−11p(t)q(t)dt, let U=R[x]≤2. Find PU(x4) and d(x4,U). Hint: the orthogonal basis of @exm-best-quadratic-approximation still works.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: C1: Perp turns sums into intersections
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title_html: C1: Perp turns sums into intersections
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html:
Let U and W be subspaces of an inner product space V.

  1. Prove that (U+W)⊥=U⊥∩W⊥. (No finiteness is needed.)
  2. Assume now that V is finite-dimensional. Deduce that (U∩W)⊥=U⊥+W⊥.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: C2: A subspace with no orthogonal complement
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title_html: C2: A subspace with no orthogonal complement
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html:
Let V=R[x], with the coefficient inner product ⟨p,q⟩=∑k≥0akbkfor p=∑kakxk, q=∑kbkxk, a finite sum, since a polynomial has only finitely many non-zero coefficients. Let U={p∈V:p(1)=0}.

  1. Verify that ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is an inner product on V and that U is a subspace with U≠V.
  2. Prove that U⊥={0}. Conclude that U⊕U⊥≠V, so @thm-orthogonal-decomposition fails without the hypothesis that U is finite-dimensional.
  3. Explain what goes wrong geometrically by exhibiting, for each m≥1, an element pm∈U with ‖pm−1‖=1/m.

exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.title: C3: Which projections are orthogonal
exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projectio.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let P∈L(V) satisfy P2=P. Prove that the following are equivalent:

  1. P=PU for some subspace U;
  2. ⟨Pu,v⟩=⟨u,Pv⟩ for all u,v∈V;
  3. kerP=(imP)⊥.

Hint: for (b) ⇒ (c), pair a vector of kerP with Pv.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-a1.title: A1
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for p0,p1,p2,… to be a monic orthogonal polynomial sequence for an inner product on R[x].
  2. State the three-term recurrence, including the formulas for ak and bk and the starting values.
  3. True or false: bk>0 for every k≥1. Justify your answer.
  4. For ⟨p,q⟩=∫−11pq, how many roots does p7 have, of what kind, and where?
  5. True or false: for every inner product on R[x] one has ⟨xp,q⟩=⟨p,xq⟩. Justify your answer.
  6. How many nodes does a Gaussian rule need in order to integrate every polynomial of degree at most 11 exactly?

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b1.title: B1: A weighted interval
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b1.html: On R[x] put ⟨p,q⟩=∫01p(t)q(t)tdt. Compute the monic p0, p1 and p2, and verify directly that p2⊥R[x]≤1.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b2.title: B2: Two rows of the table
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b2.title_html: B2: Two rows of the table
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b2.html:
Verify the degree-1 and degree-2 entries of the table for two of the classical families.

  1. Chebyshev: w(t)=(1−t2)−1/2 on (−1,1). You may use, without proof, that ∫−11(1−t2)−1/2dt=π and ∫−11t2(1−t2)−1/2dt=π/2.
  2. Laguerre: w(t)=e−t on (0,∞). You may use, without proof, that ∫0∞tke−tdt=k!.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b3.title: B3: One more Legendre polynomial
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b3.html: Continue @exm-legendre-recurrence: compute ⟨p3,p3⟩ for p3=x3−35x, then use @thm-three-term-recurrence to find p4. Verify that ⟨p4,1⟩=⟨p4,x2⟩=0.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b4.title: B4: A two-point rule on the unit interval
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b4.title_html: B4: A two-point rule on the unit interval
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-b4.html:
Work on (0,1) with w=1. Exercise B2 of Section 2 (@exr-orthonormal-bases-b2) found the monic orthogonal polynomials 1, x−12, x2−x+16.

  1. Write down the two-point Gaussian rule for ∫01f.
  2. Check it on f=x3, and show that it fails on f=x4.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-c1.title: C1: Interlacing roots
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-c1.html:
Let w be a weight on (a,b) and let (pk) be its monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. The roots of pk are said to interlace those of pk+1 when exactly one root of pk lies strictly between each pair of consecutive roots of pk+1. This is true for every k; prove the first two cases by hand.

  1. Let r be the root of p1 and s1<s2 the roots of p2. Prove that s1<r<s2.
  2. Let u1<u2<u3 be the roots of p3. Prove that u1<s1<u2<s2<u3.

Hint: evaluate the three-term recurrence at a root.

exr-orthogonal-polynomials-c2.title: C2: The ceiling is 2k − 1
exr-orthogonal-polynomials-c2.html:
Let w be a weight on (a,b) and let k≥1.

  1. Let t1,…,tk be any k distinct real numbers and α1,…,αk any real numbers. Prove that there is an f∈R[x]≤2k with ∫abfw≠∑iαif(ti).
  2. Hence deduce that the Gaussian rule of @thm-gaussian-quadrature is exact on R[x]≤2k−1 and on no larger space R[x]≤d.

exr-orthonormal-bases-a1.title: A1
exr-orthonormal-bases-a1.html:
1. Define an orthonormal list, using the Kronecker delta, and say what an orthonormal basis is.
  2. Why is every orthonormal list linearly independent? Name the result used.
  3. Write down the coordinates of v in an orthonormal basis (e1,…,en), and state Parseval’s identity.
  4. True or false: the Gram–Schmidt process (@thm-gram-schmidt) applied to a list and to the same list in reverse order produces the same orthonormal list. Justify your answer.
  5. State the criterion for linear independence in terms of the Gram matrix.
  6. True or false: every 3-dimensional real inner product space is isometrically isomorphic to R3 with the dot product. Justify your answer.

exr-orthonormal-bases-b1.title: B1: Gram–Schmidt with numbers
exr-orthonormal-bases-b1.html:
Apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to each list, with the dot product.

  1. ((1,0,1),(1,1,0),(0,1,1)) in R3.
  2. ((1,1,0,0),(1,0,1,0),(0,0,1,1)) in R4.

exr-orthonormal-bases-b2.title: B2: Gram–Schmidt on polynomials
exr-orthonormal-bases-b2.html: In R[x]≤2 with ⟨p,q⟩=∫01p(t)q(t)dt, apply the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt to (1,x,x2). Compare the monic outputs with those of @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre and explain the difference.

exr-orthonormal-bases-b3.title: B3: Coordinates without solving a system
exr-orthonormal-bases-b3.title_html: B3: Coordinates without solving a system
exr-orthonormal-bases-b3.html:
Let e1=13(1,2,2), e2=13(2,1,−2), e3=13(2,−2,1) in R3.

  1. Write v=(1,−1,4) in this basis.
  2. Compute ‖v‖2 in two ways, and state which theorem says the answers agree.
  3. Compute ⟨v,u⟩ for u=(3,0,3) from the coordinates of v and u, using @exm-orthonormal-coordinates-r3 for u.

exr-orthonormal-bases-b4.title: B4: Gram matrices
exr-orthonormal-bases-b4.html:
For each list, write down the Gram matrix and use it to decide whether the list is independent.

  1. ((1,1,0),(1,0,1),(0,1,1)) in R3 with the dot product.
  2. ((1,i),(i,1)) in C2 with the standard inner product.
  3. (1,x,x2−13) in R[x]≤2 with ⟨p,q⟩=∫−11pq.

exr-orthonormal-bases-c1.title: C1: The Gram matrix determines the list
exr-orthonormal-bases-c1.title_html: C1: The Gram matrix determines the list
exr-orthonormal-bases-c1.html:
Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space V and (w1,…,wk) a list in an inner product space W, both over F, with the same Gram matrix: ⟨vj,vi⟩=⟨wj,wi⟩ for all i,j.

  1. Prove that ∑jxjvj=0 if and only if ∑jxjwj=0, for every x∈Fk.
  2. Deduce that there is a well-defined isomorphism T:span(v1,…,vk)→span(w1,…,wk) with Tvj=wj for every j.
  3. Prove that T is an isometric isomorphism, that is, ⟨Tu,Tu′⟩=⟨u,u′⟩ for all u,u′ in the domain.

exr-orthonormal-bases-c2.title: C2: Gram–Schmidt on a dependent list
exr-orthonormal-bases-c2.title_html: C2: Gram–Schmidt on a dependent list
exr-orthonormal-bases-c2.html:
Let (v1,…,vm) be a list in an inner product space, not assumed independent, and run the recursion of @thm-gram-schmidt.

  1. Let k be the smallest index with vk∈span(v1,…,vk−1). Prove that the recursion is defined up to ek−1 and that wk=0, so the step ek=wk/‖wk‖ fails.
  2. Repair the process: show that if, whenever wk=0, we discard vk and continue with vk+1, the output is an orthonormal basis of span(v1,…,vm).
  3. Run the repaired process on ((1,1,0),(2,2,0),(1,0,1)) in R3.

exr-qr-and-householder-a1.title: A1
exr-qr-and-householder-a1.html:
1. State @thm-qr-factorization in full, including the two normalizations that make Q and R unique.
  2. Which hypothesis on A does @thm-qr-factorization need, and which does @thm-qr-householder need? Explain the difference in one sentence.
  3. Write down the Householder reflection determined by w, and list three of its properties.
  4. In @thm-householder-maps-vector, which of the two possible targets ±‖x‖e1 is chosen, and why?
  5. True or false: applying reflections on both sides, as in @thm-hessenberg-form, can be pushed to make every complex matrix unitarily similar to an upper triangular one. Justify your answer.
  6. Why must the reflection used at step k of @thm-hessenberg-form fix e1,…,ek?

exr-qr-and-householder-b1.title: B1: QR by Gram–Schmidt
exr-qr-and-householder-b1.html: Find the QR factorization of A=(111110100) in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization, and verify that R=Q⊤A for the top-left 2×2 entries.

exr-qr-and-householder-b2.title: B2: The same matrix by reflections
exr-qr-and-householder-b2.title_html: B2: The same matrix by reflections
exr-qr-and-householder-b2.html:
Let A=(112123), the matrix of @exm-qr-3x2.

  1. Find w1 and the reflection H1 of @thm-householder-maps-vector for the first column of A, and compute H1A.
  2. Find the second reflection and hence a factorization A=QR with Q∈M3(R) orthogonal and R∈M3×2(R) upper triangular.
  3. Compare the R of (b) with the R of @exm-qr-3x2, and say exactly how the two factorizations differ.

exr-qr-and-householder-b3.title: B3: A least-squares fit through QR
exr-qr-and-householder-b3.title_html: B3: A least-squares fit through QR
exr-qr-and-householder-b3.html: Fit a line y=c0+c1t to the data (t,y)=(0,1),(1,3),(2,2) in the least-squares sense, by finding the QR factorization of the design matrix and solving Rx=Q⊤b. Compute the residual and check the answer against the normal equations.

exr-qr-and-householder-b4.title: B4: Determine which are QR factorizations
exr-qr-and-householder-b4.title_html: B4: Determine which are QR factorizations
exr-qr-and-householder-b4.html:
Determine which of the following are QR factorizations of the matrix on the left in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization. Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the clause that fails and repair it if possible.

  1. (3147)=15(3−443)(53150175).
  2. (1011)=(1−111)(112012).
  3. (−1001)=(1001)(−1001).

exr-qr-and-householder-c1.title: C1: All the QR factorizations of a matrix
exr-qr-and-householder-c1.title_html: C1: All the QR factorizations of a matrix
exr-qr-and-householder-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have independent columns, with QR factorization A=QR as in @thm-qr-factorization.

  1. Prove that an upper triangular S∈Mn(F) with S∗S=In is diagonal, with diagonal entries of modulus 1.
  2. Deduce that the pairs (Q1,R1) with Q1∗Q1=In, R1 upper triangular and invertible, and A=Q1R1, are exactly the pairs (QD−1,DR) for D=diag(d1,…,dn) with |dk|=1.
  3. Hence give a second proof of the uniqueness statement of @thm-qr-factorization.

exr-qr-and-householder-c2.title: C2: Reflections do not mind dependence
exr-qr-and-householder-c2.title_html: C2: Reflections do not mind dependence
exr-qr-and-householder-c2.html:
Let A=(112213235), whose third column is the sum of the first two.

  1. Run the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt on the columns of A and say precisely which step fails.
  2. Carry out the Householder reduction of @thm-qr-householder on A and exhibit R.
  3. Explain, using @thm-qr-factorization, why no factorization A=QR with Q∗Q=I3 and R upper triangular with positive diagonal can exist.

exr-qr-and-householder-c3.title: C3: Triangularizing with rotations
exr-qr-and-householder-c3.html:
1. Let (a,b)∈R2 be non-zero and r=a2+b2. Verify that the Givens rotation G of @def-givens-rotation with c=a/r and s=b/r satisfies G(a,b)=(r,0), and that G∈SO(2).
  2. Use (a) to write A=(3142) as QR with Q∈SO(2) and R upper triangular with positive diagonal.
  3. How many Givens rotations does it take to triangularize a general 3×3 real matrix, and which entries does each one kill? Compare with the number of Householder reflections.

exr-riesz-and-duality-a1.title: A1
exr-riesz-and-duality-a1.html:
1. State the Riesz Representation Theorem, including every hypothesis.
  2. Write down the formula for the Riesz vector of φ in terms of an orthonormal basis, and say where the conjugate comes from.
  3. True or false: over C, the Riesz map Φ:V→V∗ is a linear isomorphism. Justify your answer.
  4. In what sense does an inner product answer the question Chapter 4 left open about V≅V∗?
  5. Under Φ, which subspace of V∗ corresponds to U⊥?
  6. Give an example showing that the theorem fails in infinite dimension.

exr-riesz-and-duality-b1.title: B1: Riesz vectors for evaluation
exr-riesz-and-duality-b1.html: On V=R[x]≤2 use the node inner product ⟨p,q⟩=p(−1)q(−1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1). Find the Riesz vectors of φ(p)=p(0) and of ψ(p)=p(1).

exr-riesz-and-duality-b2.title: B2: Riesz vectors on matrices
exr-riesz-and-duality-b2.html:
On Mn(C) with the Frobenius inner product ⟨A,B⟩=tr(B∗A), find the Riesz vector of:

  1. φ(A)=a12 (assume n≥2);
  2. φC(A)=tr(CA), for a fixed C∈Mn(C).

exr-riesz-and-duality-b3.title: B3: The correspondence in \nR^4
exr-riesz-and-duality-b3.title_html: B3: The correspondence in R4
exr-riesz-and-duality-b3.html: In R4 with the dot product, let U=span((1,0,1,0),(0,1,0,1)). Find a basis of U⊥ and a basis of U0, and verify that Φ carries the first to the second.

exr-riesz-and-duality-c1.title: C1: Riesz without an orthonormal basis
exr-riesz-and-duality-c1.title_html: C1: Riesz without an orthonormal basis
exr-riesz-and-duality-c1.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let φ∈V∗ be non-zero. Write K=kerφ.

  1. Prove that dim⁡K⊥=1.
  2. Let u span K⊥ with ‖u‖=1. Prove that w=φ(u)―u satisfies φ(v)=⟨v,w⟩ for all v∈V.
  3. Deduce @thm-riesz-representation, including the case φ=0.

Hint for (b): split v using V=K⊕K⊥.

exr-riesz-and-duality-c2.title: C2: Evaluation at 0 is not represented
exr-riesz-and-duality-c2.title_html: C2: Evaluation at 0 is not represented
exr-riesz-and-duality-c2.html:
Let V=R[x] with ⟨p,q⟩=∫01p(t)q(t)dt, and let φ(p)=p(0). Suppose, for a contradiction, that w=∑j=0dcjxj satisfied ⟨p,w⟩=p(0) for every p∈V.

  1. Show that ∑j=0dcjk+j+1=0 for every integer k≥1, and that the same sum equals 1 for k=0.
  2. Let N(s)=∑j=0dcj∏i≠j(s+i+1), the product running over i∈{0,…,d}∖{j}. Show that N(k)=0 for every integer k≥1, and deduce that N is the zero polynomial.
  3. Deduce that every cj=0, and hence a contradiction.

lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing.title: Moving a matrix across the inner product
lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing.title_html: Moving a matrix across the inner product
lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then for all x∈Fn and y∈Fm, ⟨Ax,y⟩=⟨x,A∗y⟩,⟨y,Ax⟩=⟨A∗y,x⟩.

lem-even-multiplicity-no-sign-change.title: Even multiplicities mean no sign change
lem-even-multiplicity-no-sign-change.title_html: Even multiplicities mean no sign change
lem-even-multiplicity-no-sign-change.html: Let I⊆R be an open interval and let f∈R[x] be non-zero. If multr(f) is even for every r∈I, then f≥0 throughout I, or f≤0 throughout I.

lem-kernel-normal-equations.title: The null space of \A^{*}\A
lem-kernel-normal-equations.title_html: The null space of A∗A
lem-kernel-normal-equations.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then nul(A∗A)=nul(A).

lem-polarization-identities.title: Polarization Identities
lem-polarization-identities.html:
Let V be an inner product space over F and let u,v∈V.

  1. If F=R, then ⟨u,v⟩=14(‖u+v‖2−‖u−v‖2).
  2. If F=C, then ⟨u,v⟩=14∑k=03ik‖u+ikv‖2.

prp-householder-properties.title: Properties of a Householder Reflection
prp-householder-properties.html:
Let w∈Fm be non-zero and H=Hw. Then

  1. H∗=H (H is Hermitian);
  2. H2=Im, so H−1=H;
  3. H is unitary;
  4. Hw=−w, and Hv=v for every v⊥w;
  5. detH=−1.

prp-isometry-eigenvalues-modulus-one.title: Eigenvalues of an Isometry Have Modulus 1
prp-isometry-eigenvalues-modulus-one.title_html: Eigenvalues of an Isometry Have Modulus 1
prp-isometry-eigenvalues-modulus-one.html: Let T∈L(V) be an isometry of an inner product space over F, and let λ∈F be an eigenvalue of T. Then |λ|=1. In particular, if F=R then λ=1 or λ=−1.

prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence.title: Existence and uniqueness of the monic sequence
prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence.title_html: Existence and uniqueness of the monic sequence
prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence.html: Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ be an inner product on R[x]. For each k∈N there is exactly one monic pk of degree k with ⟨pk,q⟩=0 for every q∈R[x]≤k−1. These pk form the unique monic orthogonal polynomial sequence, and (p0,…,pk) is an orthogonal basis of R[x]≤k for every k. The same holds on R[x]≤n for k≤n.

prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric.title: Multiplication by x is symmetric
prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric.html: Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ be an inner product on R[x] coming from a weight, or the node inner product on R[x]≤n. Then ⟨xp,q⟩=⟨p,xq⟩ for all polynomials p,q in the space (in the node case, for all p,q of degree at most n−1, so that xp and xq still lie in it).

prp-orthogonal-complement-subspace.title: Perp is always a subspace
prp-orthogonal-complement-subspace.html: For every subset S of an inner product space V, the set S⊥ is a subspace of V. Moreover S⊥=span(S)⊥.

prp-orthogonal-group-properties.title: The Groups and Their Determinants
prp-orthogonal-group-properties.html:
1. U(n) and O(n) are groups under matrix multiplication, and O(n)=U(n)∩Mn(R).
  2. If A∈U(n) then |detA|=1. If A∈O(n) then detA=1 or detA=−1.
  3. SO(n) is a subgroup of O(n).

prp-self-adjoint-immediate.title: First Properties of Self-adjoint Operators
prp-self-adjoint-immediate.html:
Let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional inner product space V over F.

  1. ⟨Tv,v⟩∈R for every v∈V, even when F=C.
  2. If B is an orthonormal basis of V, the diagonal entries of [T]BB are real.
  3. T is normal.

thm-adjoint-exists.title: Existence and Uniqueness of the Adjoint
thm-adjoint-exists.title_html: Existence and Uniqueness of the Adjoint
thm-adjoint-exists.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, and let T∈L(V,W). Then there is exactly one map T∗:W→V such that ⟨Tv,w⟩W=⟨v,T∗w⟩Vfor all v∈V, w∈W, and this T∗ is linear.

thm-adjoint-properties.title: Properties of the Adjoint
thm-adjoint-properties.html:
Let U,V,W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F.

  1. For S,T∈L(V,W), (S+T)∗=S∗+T∗.
  2. For T∈L(V,W) and c∈F, (cT)∗=c―T∗.
  3. For T∈L(U,V) and S∈L(V,W), (ST)∗=T∗S∗.
  4. T∗∗=T for every T∈L(V,W), and (idV)∗=idV.
  5. If T∈L(V,W) is invertible, then T∗ is invertible and (T∗)−1=(T−1)∗.

thm-adjoint-vs-dual.title: The Adjoint Is the Dual Map Read Through Riesz
thm-adjoint-vs-dual.title_html: The Adjoint Is the Dual Map Read Through Riesz
thm-adjoint-vs-dual.html: Let V,W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F and T∈L(V,W). Then ΦV∘T∗=T′∘ΦW.

thm-annihilator-vs-orthogonal-complement.title: Perp corresponds to the annihilator
thm-annihilator-vs-orthogonal-complement.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F, let U be a subspace and let Φ be the Riesz map. Then Φ(U⊥)=U0. Equivalently, a functional φ∈V∗ annihilates U if and only if its Riesz vector lies in U⊥.

thm-bessel-inequality.title: Bessel’s Inequality
thm-bessel-inequality.html: Let V be an inner product space over F, not assumed finite-dimensional, and let (e1,…,ek) be an orthonormal list in V. Then for every v∈V, ∑i=1k|⟨v,ei⟩|2≤‖v‖2.

thm-best-approximation.title: Best Approximation Theorem
thm-best-approximation.html: Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V, and let v∈V. Then ‖v−PUv‖≤‖v−u‖for every u∈U, and equality holds only for u=PUv.

thm-cauchy-schwarz.title: Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
thm-cauchy-schwarz.html: Let V be an inner product space and u,v∈V. Then |⟨u,v⟩|≤‖u‖‖v‖, with equality if and only if the list (u,v) is linearly dependent.

thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal.html:
Let V,W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F and let T∈L(V,W). Then

  1. kerT∗=(imT)⊥;
  2. imT∗=(kerT)⊥;
  3. V=kerT⊕imT∗;
  4. W=imT⊕kerT∗.

thm-fourier-best-approximation.title: Fourier Partial Sums Are Best Approximations
thm-fourier-best-approximation.title_html: Fourier Partial Sums Are Best Approximations
thm-fourier-best-approximation.html:
Let f∈C[−π,π], let n≥1, and let ak,bk be the Fourier coefficients of f. Put Snf=a02+∑k=1n(akcos⁡kx+bksin⁡kx). Then, with ⟨f,g⟩=1π∫−ππfg:

  1. Snf=PWnf;
  2. ‖f−Snf‖≤‖f−g‖ for every g∈Wn, with equality only for g=Snf;
  3. a022+∑k=1n(ak2+bk2)≤1π∫−ππf(t)2dt.

thm-gaussian-quadrature.title: Gaussian Quadrature
thm-gaussian-quadrature.html: Let w be a weight on (a,b) with ⟨p,q⟩=∫abpqw, let k≥1, and let t1<⋯<tk be the roots of the monic orthogonal polynomial pk, which lie in (a,b) by @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots. Let ℓ1,…,ℓk∈R[x]≤k−1 be the Lagrange polynomials for these nodes (@def-lagrange-basis) and set αi=∫abℓi(t)w(t)dt(i=1,…,k). Then every αi is strictly positive, and ∫abf(t)w(t)dt=∑i=1kαif(ti) for every f∈R[x]≤2k−1.

thm-gram-matrix-properties.title: Properties of the Gram Matrix
thm-gram-matrix-properties.html:
Let (v1,…,vk) be a list in an inner product space V over F, with Gram matrix G. Then:

  1. G is Hermitian, G∗=G, and its diagonal entries are the real numbers ‖vi‖2≥0;
  2. x∗Gx=‖∑jxjvj‖2 for every x∈Fk;
  3. G is invertible if and only if (v1,…,vk) is linearly independent;
  4. detG is a real number with detG≥0, and detG>0 exactly when the list is linearly independent.

thm-gram-schmidt.title: Gram–Schmidt Process
thm-gram-schmidt.html:
Let V be an inner product space and let (v1,…,vm) be a linearly independent list in V. Define recursively wk=vk−∑i=1k−1⟨vk,ei⟩ei,ek=wk‖wk‖(k=1,…,m). Then every wk is non-zero, so the recursion is defined, and:

  1. (e1,…,em) is an orthonormal list;
  2. span(e1,…,ek)=span(v1,…,vk) for every k=1,…,m;
  3. if (v1,…,vr) is already orthonormal for some r≤m, then ei=vi for i≤r.

In particular, every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

thm-hessenberg-form.title: Reduction to Hessenberg Form
thm-hessenberg-form.html: Let A∈Mn(F), n≥1. Then there is a unitary Q∈Mn(F) such that Z=Q∗AQ is upper Hessenberg, that is, zij=0whenever i>j+1. The matrix Q can be taken to be a product of n−2 factors, each a Householder reflection or an identity matrix (and Q=In when n≤2). For n=4 the pattern is Z=(∗∗∗∗∗∗∗∗0∗∗∗00∗∗).

thm-householder-maps-vector.title: A Reflection Flattening a Vector
thm-householder-maps-vector.html: Let x∈Fm be non-zero, and let α={x1/|x1|,x1≠0,1,x1=0,w=x+α‖x‖e1. Then w≠0 and Hwx=−α‖x‖e1. In particular Hwx is a multiple of e1 of length ‖x‖. Over R, α is the sign of x1 (or 1 if x1=0), and Hwx=∓‖x‖e1 according to that sign.

thm-inner-product-basic-properties.title: First Properties of an Inner Product
thm-inner-product-basic-properties.title_html: First Properties of an Inner Product
thm-inner-product-basic-properties.html:
Let V be an inner product space over F. For all u,v,w∈V and a,b∈F:

  1. ⟨v,v⟩ is a real number, and ⟨v,v⟩≥0 with equality if and only if v=0;
  2. ⟨u,av+bw⟩=a―⟨u,v⟩+b―⟨u,w⟩ (conjugate-linear in the second slot);
  3. ⟨0,v⟩=⟨v,0⟩=0;
  4. if ⟨u,w⟩=⟨v,w⟩ for every w∈V, then u=v.

thm-isometry-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Isometries
thm-isometry-characterizations.html:
Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, and let T∈L(V,W). The following are equivalent.

  1. T is an isometry: ‖Tv‖=‖v‖ for every v∈V.
  2. T preserves inner products: ⟨Tu,Tv⟩=⟨u,v⟩ for all u,v∈V.
  3. T∗T=idV.
  4. T sends every orthonormal list in V to an orthonormal list in W.
  5. T sends some orthonormal basis of V to an orthonormal list in W.
  6. For one (equivalently every) pair of orthonormal bases B of V and C of W, the matrix A=[T]BC∈Mm×n(F), where n=dim⁡V and m=dim⁡W, satisfies A∗A=In; that is, the n columns of A are orthonormal vectors of Fm.

If in addition dim⁡W=dim⁡V, then (a)–(f) are further equivalent to each of

  1. T is invertible with T−1=T∗;
  2. TT∗=idW.

thm-least-squares.title: Least Squares Theorem
thm-least-squares.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and b∈Fm, and write U=col(A). For x∈Fn, the following are equivalent:

  1. ‖Ax−b‖≤‖Az−b‖ for every z∈Fn;
  2. Ax=PUb;
  3. A∗Ax=A∗b.

Moreover such an x always exists. A vector satisfying these conditions is called a least-squares solution of Ax=b, and the equations in (c) are the normal equations.

thm-matrix-of-adjoint.title: The Matrix of the Adjoint Is the Conjugate Transpose
thm-matrix-of-adjoint.title_html: The Matrix of the Adjoint Is the Conjugate Transpose
thm-matrix-of-adjoint.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, let B=(v1,…,vn) be an orthonormal basis of V and C=(w1,…,wm) an orthonormal basis of W, and let T∈L(V,W). Then [T∗]CB=([T]BC)∗.

thm-minimum-norm-solution.title: Minimum-Norm Solution
thm-minimum-norm-solution.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) and let b∈Fm be such that Ax=b is consistent. Write K=nul(A). Then:

  1. exactly one solution xmin of Ax=b lies in K⊥;
  2. ‖xmin‖<‖x‖ for every other solution x.

We call xmin the minimum-norm solution.

thm-norm-properties.title: Properties of the Induced Norm
thm-norm-properties.html:
Let V be an inner product space over F, u,v∈V and c∈F. Then:

  1. ‖v‖≥0, with ‖v‖=0 if and only if v=0;
  2. ‖cv‖=|c|‖v‖;
  3. ‖u+v‖2=‖u‖2+2Re⟨u,v⟩+‖v‖2.

thm-orthogonal-2x2.title: Classification of the Plane Isometries
thm-orthogonal-2x2.html:
Let A∈O(2).

  1. If detA=1, then A=Rθ for a unique θ∈[0,2π).
  2. If detA=−1, then A=Mθ for a unique θ∈[0,2π). In this case A2=I, the eigenvalues of A are 1 and −1, and A is the reflection in the line L=span((cos⁡θ2,sin⁡θ2)): it fixes L pointwise and negates L⊥.

Consequently O(2)={Rθ}∪{Mθ}, and SO(2)={Rθ:θ∈[0,2π)}.

thm-orthogonal-decomposition.title: Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem
thm-orthogonal-decomposition.html:
Let V be an inner product space over F and let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of V. Then:

  1. V=U⊕U⊥;
  2. (U⊥)⊥=U;
  3. if in addition V is finite-dimensional, then dim⁡U⊥=dim⁡V−dim⁡U.

thm-orthogonal-independent.title: Orthogonal Non-zero Vectors Are Independent
thm-orthogonal-independent.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be an orthogonal list of non-zero vectors in an inner product space. Then the list is linearly independent.

thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots.title: Roots of an Orthogonal Polynomial
thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots.html: Let w be a weight on (a,b), let ⟨p,q⟩=∫abpqw, and let (pk) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. For every k≥1, the polynomial pk has k distinct real roots, and every one of them lies in the open interval (a,b).

thm-orthonormal-coordinates.title: Coordinates, Inner Products and Norms in an Orthonormal Basis
thm-orthonormal-coordinates.title_html: Coordinates, Inner Products and Norms in an Orthonormal Basis
thm-orthonormal-coordinates.html:
Let (e1,…,en) be an orthonormal basis of an inner product space V, and let u,v∈V. Then:

  1. v=∑i=1n⟨v,ei⟩ei;
  2. ⟨u,v⟩=∑i=1n⟨u,ei⟩⟨v,ei⟩―;
  3. ‖v‖2=∑i=1n|⟨v,ei⟩|2 (Parseval’s identity for a finite orthonormal basis).

thm-parseval-identity.title: Parseval’s Identity
thm-parseval-identity.html: Let (e1,…,ek) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space V and let v∈V. Then ∑i=1k|⟨v,ei⟩|2=‖v‖2if and only ifv∈span(e1,…,ek). In particular, if (e1,…,ek) is an orthonormal basis of V, the identity holds for every v∈V.

thm-projection-formula.title: Projection formula
thm-projection-formula.html:
Let U be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space V, with orthonormal basis (e1,…,ek). Then for every v∈V:

  1. PUv=∑i=1k⟨v,ei⟩ei;
  2. ⟨PUu,v⟩=⟨u,PUv⟩ for all u,v∈V;
  3. ‖PUv‖≤‖v‖, with equality if and only if v∈U.

thm-pythagoras.title: Pythagorean Theorem
thm-pythagoras.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be an orthogonal list in an inner product space. Then ‖v1+⋯+vk‖2=‖v1‖2+⋯+‖vk‖2.

thm-qr-factorization.title: QR Factorization
thm-qr-factorization.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have linearly independent columns. Then there are matrices Q∈Mm×n(F) and R∈Mn(F) with

  1. the columns of Q orthonormal, equivalently Q∗Q=In;
  2. R upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries;
  3. A=QR.

Moreover Q and R are unique: any pair satisfying (a), (b), (c) is this one. The pair (Q,R) is the QR factorization of A.

thm-qr-householder.title: QR by Householder Reflections
thm-qr-householder.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F). Then there are a unitary Q∈Mm(F) and an R∈Mm×n(F) with rij=0 whenever i>j, such that A=QR. Moreover Q can be taken to be a product of at most min(n,m−1) Householder reflections. No hypothesis on the columns of A is needed.

thm-riesz-representation.title: Riesz Representation Theorem
thm-riesz-representation.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let φ∈V∗. Then there is a unique w∈V such that φ(v)=⟨v,w⟩for every v∈V. If (e1,…,en) is any orthonormal basis of V, then w=∑i=1nφ(ei)―ei.

thm-rigid-motion-linear.title: Distance-Preserving Maps Are Affine
thm-rigid-motion-linear.html:
Let f:Rn→Rn be any function, not assumed linear, with ‖f(x)−f(y)‖=‖x−y‖for all x,y∈Rn.

  1. If f(0)=0, then f is linear and orthogonal.
  2. In general, f(x)=Ax+b for a unique A∈O(n) and a unique b∈Rn.

thm-so3-rotation.title: Every Element of SO(3) Is a Rotation
thm-so3-rotation.title_html: Every Element of SO(3) Is a Rotation
thm-so3-rotation.html: Let A∈SO(3). Then there is a unit vector u∈R3 with Au=u, and an orthonormal basis B=(u,w1,w2) of R3 in which [TA]BB=(1000cos⁡θ−sin⁡θ0sin⁡θcos⁡θ) for some θ. That is, A fixes the axis span(u) and rotates the plane span(u)⊥ by θ. Moreover trA=1+2cos⁡θ.

thm-three-term-recurrence.title: Three-Term Recurrence
thm-three-term-recurrence.html: Let (pk) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence of @prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence, for an inner product satisfying @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric. For a weight on an interval this covers every k; for the node inner product on n nodes, where @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric holds only up to degree n−1, read the statement for k+1≤n. Put p−1=0 and, for k≥0, ak=⟨xpk,pk⟩⟨pk,pk⟩,bk=⟨pk,pk⟩⟨pk−1,pk−1⟩  (k≥1). Then p0=1, p1=x−a0, and pk+1=(x−ak)pk−bkpk−1for every k≥1. Moreover bk>0 for every k≥1.
